stem: A certain book has 250 pages, and 21 of these pages have an illustration. If one of the book’s pages is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a page with an illustration? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.)
whyCorrect: Probability is just the count you want over the total count. Here that is 21 illustrated pages out of 250 pages, so the probability is \( \frac{21}{250} \), which is 0.084 as a decimal. The wording only warns you not to convert to a percent — do not write 8.4.
note: Grid-in; 21/250 and 0.084 are both acceptable forms.

stem: There are 20 marbles in a bag: 8 red marbles, 10 green marbles, and 2 blue marbles. If one of these marbles is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a red marble?
whyCorrect: Count the red marbles and divide by the total number of marbles. There are 8 red out of 20 total, so the probability is \( \frac{8}{20} \). The denominator is always the whole bag, not the marbles of the other colours.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{2}{20} \) is the probability of a blue marble.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{10}{20} \) is the probability of a green marble.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{12}{20} \) counts everything that is not red (10 green + 2 blue), which is the complement of what was asked.

stem: A choir of 48 singers has 12 members who sing bass. If one singer from the choir is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a singer who sings bass?
whyCorrect: Divide the number of bass singers by the total number of singers: 12 out of 48, so \( \frac{12}{48} \). You do not need to reduce it — the choices are all written over 48.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{1}{48} \) is the probability of picking one specific named singer, not any of the 12 basses.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{36}{48} \) is the probability of selecting a singer who does not sing bass.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{48}{48} \) says every singer sings bass, which contradicts the stem.

If a person in this city is selected at random, which of the following is closest to the probability of selecting a person who is greater than 65 years old, given that the person is at least 18 years old?
whyCorrect: The phrase "given that the person is at least 18" shrinks the pool: you are no longer dividing by everyone, only by the people 18 and over. That group is 24% + 28% + 21% = 73%. The over-65 share of it is \( \frac{21}{73} \approx 0.288 \), closest to 0.29.

whyWrong.A: 0.21 is the unconditional probability — it divides by the whole city, ignoring the condition that the person is at least 18.
whyWrong.C: 0.35 is roughly \( \frac{21}{60} \), which comes from leaving out one of the adult age bands when building the new total.
whyWrong.D: 0.41 is roughly \( \frac{21}{51} \), the over-65 group compared with only the 41–65 band plus itself.

stem: A sleep study consisted of 59 participants, of which 53 participants each had an average of more than 120 minutes of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep per night. If a participant from this study is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a participant that had an average of more than 120 minutes of REM sleep per night?
whyCorrect: The denominator of a probability is the size of the group you are choosing from, which here is the 59 participants in the study — not 100. The numerator is the 53 who met the REM condition, so the probability is \( \frac{53}{59} \).

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{53}{100} \) treats the study as if it had 100 participants; nothing in the stem is out of 100.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{59}{100} \) uses the total group size as the numerator and an invented denominator of 100.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{59}{53} \) inverts the fraction. A probability can never exceed 1, so this is impossible on sight.

stem: Hakim has a bag of 50 tiles, where 45 are labeled with a letter and 5 are black. If Hakim selects a tile from the bag at random, what is the probability of selecting a black tile? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.)
whyCorrect: Only the black tiles and the total matter. There are 5 black tiles out of 50, so the probability is \( \frac{5}{50} = 0.1 \). The 45 lettered tiles are there to be subtracted from or ignored, not divided by.
note: The book prints "a black tie"; corrected to "tile". 1/10 and 0.1 are both acceptable forms.

stem: The dot plot shows the estimated market values, in thousands of dollars, for 15 houses in a neighborhood. What is the maximum estimated market value, in thousands of dollars, for the data set?
whyCorrect: The maximum is just the largest value in the data set, which on a dot plot is the position of the rightmost dot — you do not need to count how many dots sit above it. That rightmost stack sits at 178, so the maximum estimated market value is 178 thousand dollars.
note: Dot plot needed. Measured from the page image, axis labelled 168 to 178 with a tick every 2 units and dots placed at whole numbers: 167 (1 dot), 168 (3), 170 (1), 171 (3), 173 (4), 174 (1), 178 (2) — 15 dots in total, matching the stated 15 houses.

stem: The dot plot shows the 9 values of a data set with a mean value of \( a \) and a median value of \( b \). The value of 46 is removed to create a new data set of 8 values with a mean value of \( y \) and a median value of \( z \). Which statement best compares the mean values and the median values for the two data sets?
whyCorrect: Removing 46 removes a clear outlier that sits far above everything else, so the mean must drop: \( a > y \). The median barely notices, because the middle of the list does not move — with 9 values the median is the 5th value, 40, and with 8 values it is the average of the 4th and 5th, which are both 40. So \( b = z \). Numerically \( a = \frac{363}{9} \approx 40.3 \) and \( y = \frac{317}{8} \approx 39.6 \).

whyWrong.A: Removing a value can only leave the mean unchanged if that value equals the mean; 46 is well above it, so \( a = y \) fails. The median also does not rise.
whyWrong.B: Same problem with \( a = y \), and the median stays at 40 rather than falling.
whyWrong.C: This has the mean going up. Deleting the largest value cannot increase the mean of what is left.

note: Dot plot needed. Measured from the page image, axis 38 to 46 with a tick at every integer: 38 (2 dots), 39 (1), 40 (3), 41 (2), 46 (1) — 9 values in total, i.e. 38, 38, 39, 40, 40, 40, 41, 41, 46. The book's stem ends without a question mark.

stem: The ratio of a person’s weight on Earth to the person’s weight on the Moon is constant. An astronaut who weighs 540 newtons on Earth weighs 90 newtons on the Moon. Another astronaut weighs \( w \) newtons on Earth. Which of the following expressions represents this astronaut’s weight, in newtons, on the Moon?
whyCorrect: Use the given pair to find the constant factor: \( \frac{90}{540} = \frac{1}{6} \), so Moon weight is Earth weight divided by 6. Applying the same factor to \( w \) gives \( \frac{w}{6} \). Check the direction against the numbers — the Moon figure must be the smaller one.

whyWrong.A: \( 6w \) multiplies instead of divides, which would make the astronaut six times heavier on the Moon.
whyWrong.B: \( 0.6w \) comes from reading the ratio as 0.6 rather than \( \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167 \); it would give 324 newtons for the first astronaut, not 90.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{6}{w} \) puts the variable in the denominator, so a heavier astronaut would weigh less on the Moon.

stem: Jaqueline spent $150 for supplies and gas to start a lawn-mowing service. She charges $25 for each lawn she mows. In the first week Jaqueline made $50 after the cost of supplies and gas was deducted. Which equation represents this situation, where \( x \) is the number of lawns Jaqueline mowed during the first week?
whyCorrect: Money in is 25 per lawn, so \( 25x \); the 150 startup cost is money out, so it is subtracted. "Made $50 after the cost was deducted" means what is left after that subtraction equals 50, giving 25x − 150 = 50.

whyWrong.B: This subtracts her earnings from the $50 profit and sets the result equal to the cost, reversing which quantity is the leftover.
whyWrong.C: This subtracts her earnings from the startup cost, treating the $150 as income and the mowing as an expense.
whyWrong.D: This adds the profit to her earnings and sets the total equal to the cost, so the $150 ends up on the income side.

stem: If 2x + 3 = 9, what is the value of 4x − 4?
whyCorrect: Solve the given equation first: 2x = 6, so x = 3. Then substitute into the second expression: 4(3) − 4 = 8. You can also notice that 4x = 2(2x) = 2(6) = 12, so 4x − 4 = 8 without finding x at all.

stem: A total of 6 squares each have side length \( r \). A total of 3 equilateral triangles each have side length \( t \). None of these squares and triangles shares a side. The sum of the perimeters of all these squares and triangles is 75. Which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: One square has perimeter 4r because a square has four equal sides, so 6 squares contribute 6(4r) = 24r. One equilateral triangle has perimeter 3t, so 3 triangles contribute 3(3t) = 9t. Setting the total equal to 75 gives 24r + 9t = 75.

whyWrong.A: 18r + 12t swaps the two shapes' side counts — it uses 3 sides per square (6 × 3) and 4 per triangle (3 × 4).
whyWrong.C: 3r + 6t uses the counts of the shapes as coefficients but attaches each to the wrong shape, and it never multiplies by the number of sides.
whyWrong.D: 6r + 3t is just the number of squares and triangles times one side each, so it adds up one side per shape rather than whole perimeters.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to 15(x + 10)?
whyCorrect: Distributing means the 15 multiplies both terms inside the parentheses: 15 · x and 15 · 10. That gives 15x + 150.

whyWrong.A: 15x + 10 multiplies only the x and leaves the 10 untouched.
whyWrong.C: 15x + 25 adds 15 and 10 instead of multiplying them.
whyWrong.D: 15x + 5 subtracts 10 from 15, which is not part of distributing at all.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to 16(x + 5)?
whyCorrect: The 16 distributes across both terms: 16 · x = 16x and 16 · 5 = 80, so the expression is 16x + 80.

whyWrong.A: 16x + 5 leaves the 5 unmultiplied.
whyWrong.C: 16x + 21 adds 16 and 5 rather than multiplying them.
whyWrong.D: 16x + 11 subtracts 5 from 16, which has nothing to do with the distributive property.

stem: \[ x = 2a(b + 5) \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( a \), \( b \), and \( x \). Which equation correctly expresses \( a \) in terms of \( b \) and \( x \)?
whyCorrect: On the right side \( a \) is multiplied by the whole quantity \( 2(b + 5) \), so to isolate \( a \) you divide both sides by that entire quantity, not just part of it. That gives \( a = \frac{x}{2(b + 5)} \).

whyWrong.A: This subtracts \( b + 5 \) instead of dividing by it. Subtraction undoes addition, but \( a \) is being multiplied here.
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of the correct expression — it divides \( 2(b + 5) \) by \( x \) instead of the other way round.
whyWrong.D: This multiplies by \( 2(b + 5) \) again rather than dividing, moving \( a \) further from being isolated.

stem: \[ x = 2a(b + 3) \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( x \), \( a \), and \( b \). Which equation correctly expresses \( a \) in terms of \( b \) and \( x \)?
whyCorrect: \( a \) is multiplied by \( 2(b + 3) \), so dividing both sides by that whole quantity isolates it: \( a = \frac{x}{2(b + 3)} \). The parentheses have to stay in the denominator, or you are only dividing by the 2.

whyWrong.A: This tries to undo multiplication with subtraction, and the \( 4b \) does not come from anywhere in the equation.
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of the correct answer, which would make \( a \) shrink as \( x \) grows.

stem: A piece of string with a length of 35 inches is cut into two parts. One part has a length of \( x \) inches, and the other part has a length of \( y \) inches. The value of \( x \) is 5 more than 2 times the value of \( y \). What is the value of \( x \)?
whyCorrect: Two facts give two equations: the pieces make up the whole string, so x + y = 35, and "5 more than 2 times y" means x = 2y + 5. Substitute the second into the first: (2y + 5) + y = 35, so 3y = 30 and y = 10. Then x = 2(10) + 5 = 25. Check: 25 + 10 = 35.

\[ a = 3k + 4r \quad \text{and} \quad b = 9k - 12r + 6, \]which expression is equivalent to \( a - b \)?
whyCorrect: The subtraction sign applies to every term of \( b \), not just the first: \( a - b = 3k + 4r - 9k + 12r - 6 \). Combining like terms gives \( -6k + 16r - 6 \). The place people lose the question is the \( -12r \), which becomes \( +12r \).

whyWrong.B: The \( k \) and \( r \) terms are right, but the constant kept its sign: subtracting \( +6 \) must give \( -6 \).
whyWrong.C: This subtracts only the first term of \( b \) and then adds \( -12r \) unchanged, giving \( 4r - 12r = -8r \), and it also keeps \( +6 \).
whyWrong.D: This distributes the minus sign to the constant but not to the \( -12r \) term, so both the \( r \) coefficient and the reasoning are inconsistent.

stem: \[ (9y + 9) - (5y + 7) \]The given expression is equivalent to \( by + c \), where \( b \) and \( c \) are constants. What is the value of \( b \)?
whyCorrect: Distribute the minus sign and collect like terms: \( 9y - 5y = 4y \) and \( 9 - 7 = 2 \), so the expression is \( 4y + 2 \). Matching that with \( by + c \) makes \( b = 4 \) (and \( c = 2 \)). The question asks only for the coefficient of \( y \).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to 15(x + 10)?
whyCorrect: Distribute the 15 over both terms in the parentheses: 15 · x = 15x and 15 · 10 = 150, giving 15x + 150.

whyWrong.A: 15x + 10 multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses.
whyWrong.C: 15x + 25 adds 15 and 10 rather than multiplying them.
whyWrong.D: 15x + 5 subtracts 10 from 15, which is not what distributing does.

stem: On average, a certain tree grows 51 centimeters every \( m \) months. At this rate, which expression represents the number of centimeters, on average, the tree grows every \( k \) years?
whyCorrect: Get a monthly rate first: \( \frac{51}{m} \) centimeters per month. Then convert the time, since \( k \) years is \( 12k \) months. Multiplying gives \( \frac{51}{m} \cdot 12k = \frac{612k}{m} \). Skipping the year-to-month conversion is what produces the wrong choices.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{17m}{4k} \) has \( m \) on top and \( k \) underneath, so more months per 51 cm would mean more growth — backwards. It is also \( \frac{51}{12} \) reduced, i.e. a division by 12 instead of a multiplication.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{17k}{4m} \) is \( \frac{51k}{12m} \), which divides by 12 instead of multiplying — that converts months to years, the wrong direction.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{612m}{k} \) uses the right factor of 12 but inverts the variables, so the rate rises when the tree takes longer to grow 51 cm.

stem: The total mass, in kilograms, of \( r \) identical objects is \( t \). Which expression represents the total mass, in kilograms, of \( 146r \) of these objects?
whyCorrect: You are not asked about 146 objects — you are asked about \( 146r \) objects, which is 146 groups of \( r \). Each group of \( r \) has mass \( t \), so 146 of those groups have mass \( 146t \). You never need to find the mass of a single object.

whyWrong.A: Subtracting a mass from a count of objects is not a meaningful operation, and scaling a quantity up never involves subtraction.
whyWrong.B: Same problem: adding 146 to the mass would give the mass of \( r \) objects plus 146 kg, not 146 times as many objects.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{t}{146} \) divides instead of multiplying, so it describes \( \frac{r}{146} \) objects.

stem: One gallon of sealant costs $23 and will cover 250 square feet of a surface. A deck has a total surface area of \( d \) square feet. Which of the following represents the cost \( c \), in dollars, of the sealant needed to cover the deck twice?
whyCorrect: Covering the deck twice means sealing \( 2d \) square feet, so the number of gallons is \( \frac{2d}{250} = \frac{d}{125} \). Multiply the gallons by the price per gallon: \( c = 23\left(\frac{d}{125}\right) \). Notice the 2 belongs on top of the fraction, which is why the denominator halves rather than doubles.

whyWrong.A: This divides area by price instead of multiplying price by gallons, and it ignores the second coat entirely. The units come out as square feet per dollar.
whyWrong.B: Same inverted structure as A; doubling the 250 in the numerator also has the coats working in the wrong direction.
whyWrong.D: \( 23\left(\frac{d}{250}\right) \) is the cost of covering the deck once. It needs to be doubled.

stem: \[ PC = N(44 - C) \]The given equation relates the variables \( P \), \( N \), and \( C \). Which expression represents the value of \( C \) for distinct positive values of \( P \) and \( N \)?
whyCorrect: \( C \) appears on both sides once you expand, so collect it: \( PC = 44N - NC \), then \( PC + NC = 44N \). Factor the left side as \( C(P + N) = 44N \) and divide, giving \( C = \frac{44N}{N + P} \). Factoring out \( C \) is the step being tested.

whyWrong.A: An expression for \( C \) cannot contain \( C \); this one does, so nothing has been solved.
whyWrong.B: This also still contains \( C \), on both the top and the bottom — it is just the original equation rearranged one step.
whyWrong.D: The \( +1 \) in the denominator does not come from anywhere; factoring \( C \) out of \( PC + NC \) leaves \( P + N \), not \( P + 1 \).

stem: On average, a certain tree grows 87 centimeters every \( m \) months. At this rate, which expression represents the number of centimeters, on average, the tree grows every \( k \) years?
whyCorrect: The monthly rate is \( \frac{87}{m} \) centimeters per month, and \( k \) years is \( 12k \) months. Multiplying gives \( \frac{87}{m} \cdot 12k = \frac{1{,}044k}{m} \). The conversion multiplies by 12 because a year contains more months, not fewer.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{29m}{4k} \) is \( \frac{87m}{12k} \): it divides by 12 instead of multiplying, and it puts \( m \) and \( k \) on the wrong sides of the fraction.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{29k}{4m} \) is \( \frac{87k}{12m} \), so it converts in the wrong direction — dividing by 12 rather than multiplying.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{1{,}044m}{k} \) uses the right factor of 12 but swaps \( m \) and \( k \), making growth increase when the tree grows more slowly.

stem: \[ f = \frac{(10x)^{2}}{7g} \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( f \), \( x \), and \( g \). Which equation correctly expresses \( x \) in terms of \( f \) and \( g \)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \( 7g \) to get \( 7fg = (10x)^{2} = 100x^{2} \). Then \( x^{2} = \frac{7fg}{100} \), and taking the positive square root gives \( x = \frac{\sqrt{7fg}}{10} \). The 10 is inside the square, so it comes out as 10, not \( \sqrt{10} \).

whyWrong.B: This multiplies by 10 instead of dividing — it undoes \( \frac{x}{10} \) rather than \( 10x \).
whyWrong.C: This square-roots the 10 along with everything else, but \( (10x)^{2} = 100x^{2} \), so the divisor under the root would have to be 100.
whyWrong.D: Subtracting 10 undoes addition, not multiplication; nothing in the equation adds 10.

stem: \[ q - 34r = s \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( q \), \( r \), and \( s \). Which equation correctly expresses \( q \) in terms of \( r \) and \( s \)?
whyCorrect: The term \( 34r \) is being subtracted from \( q \), so add \( 34r \) to both sides to undo it: \( q = s + 34r \).

whyWrong.A: This subtracts \( 34r \) again instead of moving it across, so it changes the equation rather than solving it.
whyWrong.C: Multiplying \( 34r \) by \( s \) treats the subtraction as if it were a division, which it is not.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the equation divides, and the negative sign has no source; check by putting sample numbers in, e.g. q = 40, r = 1, s = 6.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to 15(x + 10)?
whyCorrect: The 15 outside the parentheses multiplies every term inside: 15 · x = 15x and 15 · 10 = 150, so the result is 15x + 150.

whyWrong.A: 15x + 10 forgets to multiply the 10.
whyWrong.C: 15x + 25 comes from adding 15 and 10 instead of multiplying.
whyWrong.D: 15x + 5 comes from subtracting, which is not part of distributing.

note: Third exact copy of the same item in this book: identical to expressions-15 and expressions-40, stem and all four choices. Keep at most one.

stem: \[ P = N(34 - C) \]The given equation relates the variables \( P \), \( N \), and \( C \). Which expression represents the value of \( C \) for distinct positive values of \( P \) and \( N \)?
whyCorrect: Divide both sides by \( N \) first, which keeps the parentheses intact: \( \frac{P}{N} = 34 - C \). Then move \( C \) across and \( \frac{P}{N} \) across to get \( C = 34 - \frac{P}{N} \). Dividing before expanding is what makes this one line of work.

whyWrong.A: An expression for \( C \) cannot contain \( C \) itself, so this has not isolated anything.
whyWrong.B: The sign is wrong: \( \frac{P}{N} = 34 - C \) rearranges to \( C = 34 - \frac{P}{N} \), not \( 34 + \frac{P}{N} \).
whyWrong.C: This divides by \( C \) instead of \( N \), and it leaves \( C \) on both sides.

stem: \[ 11m = 7(n + p) \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( m \), \( n \), and \( p \). Which equation correctly gives \( n \) in terms of \( m \) and \( p \)?
whyCorrect: Divide both sides by 7 before touching the parentheses: \( \frac{11m}{7} = n + p \). Then subtract \( p \): \( n = \frac{11m}{7} - p \). Expanding to \( 11m = 7n + 7p \) works too and gives the same result.

whyWrong.A: This has no \( m \) in the numerator and no \( p \) subtraction; it does not follow from either valid route.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies by 7 instead of dividing, and adds \( p \) instead of subtracting it — both operations go the wrong way.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts 7 rather than dividing by it. The 7 multiplies the whole parenthesis, so only division removes it.

stem: One gallon of sealant costs $13 and will cover 300 square feet of a surface. A deck has a total surface area of \( d \) square feet. Which equation represents the cost \( c \), in dollars, of the sealant needed to cover the deck twice?
whyCorrect: Two coats means \( 2d \) square feet must be covered, so the gallons needed are \( \frac{2d}{300} = \frac{d}{150} \). Cost is gallons times price per gallon, so \( c = 13\left(\frac{d}{150}\right) \). Doubling the area halves the denominator, which is why 300 becomes 150.

whyWrong.A: This puts the coverage on top and the price underneath, giving square feet per dollar, and it never accounts for the second coat.
whyWrong.B: Same inverted structure, with the doubling applied to the wrong number.
whyWrong.D: \( 13\left(\frac{d}{300}\right) \) is the cost of a single coat.

stem: One gallon of sealant costs $29 and will cover 300 square feet of a surface. A deck has a total surface area of \( d \) square feet. Which equation represents the cost \( c \), in dollars, of the sealant needed to cover the deck twice?
whyCorrect: Covering twice means \( 2d \) square feet, so the gallons needed are \( \frac{2d}{300} = \frac{d}{150} \). Multiply by the $29 price per gallon: \( c = 29\left(\frac{d}{150}\right) \).

whyWrong.A: The price belongs in the numerator as a multiplier, not the denominator; this also uses one coat, not two.
whyWrong.B: Same inverted setup as A, with the 2 attached to the coverage figure instead of the area.
whyWrong.D: \( 29\left(\frac{d}{300}\right) \) covers the deck once and needs doubling.

stem: A machine makes 9-inch, 8-inch, and 3-inch parts. During a certain day, the number of 9-inch parts that the machine makes is 4 times the number \( n \) of 8-inch parts, and the number of 3-inch parts is 15. During this day, the machine makes 100 parts in total. Which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: The 100 counts parts, not inches, so the lengths 9, 8 and 3 never enter the equation — they only name the three kinds of part. The counts are \( 4n \) nine-inch parts, \( n \) eight-inch parts and 15 three-inch parts, so \( 4n + n + 15 = 100 \), which simplifies to 5n + 15 = 100.

whyWrong.A: This multiplies each count by its length, so the left side is a total length in inches while the right side is a count of parts.
whyWrong.B: This also weights by length and, worse, uses \( n \) for all three counts, ignoring both the "4 times" relationship and the 15.
whyWrong.C: This counts the 9-inch parts but drops the \( n \) eight-inch parts entirely.

note: Same template as expressions-93 (lengths and multiplier changed); flag as a near-duplicate pair at allocation.

stem: Hassan put up wire fencing along each edge of a rectangular garden with a length of \( x \) feet and a width of \( y \) feet. Hassan put up a total of 44 feet of wire fencing. Which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: Fencing along every edge is the perimeter, and a rectangle has two sides of each length, so the total is \( x + y + x + y = 2x + 2y \). Setting that equal to the 44 feet used gives 2x + 2y = 44.

whyWrong.B: x + y is only one length plus one width — half the way around the garden.
whyWrong.C: 2xy multiplies the dimensions, which produces twice the area rather than a distance.
whyWrong.D: xy is the area in square feet, so it cannot equal a length of fencing.

stem: A machine makes 8-inch, 5-inch, and 7-inch parts. During a certain day, the number of 8-inch parts that the machine makes is 3 times the number \( n \) of 5-inch parts, and the number of 7-inch parts is 12. During this day, the machine makes 100 parts total. Which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: The total of 100 is a count of parts, so the part lengths play no role in the equation. There are \( 3n \) eight-inch parts, \( n \) five-inch parts and 12 seven-inch parts, giving \( 3n + n + 12 = 100 \), i.e. 4n + 12 = 100.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying each count by its length gives a total in inches, which cannot equal a number of parts.
whyWrong.B: This weights by length and uses \( n \) for every category, throwing away both the "3 times" relationship and the 12.
whyWrong.C: This counts only the 8-inch parts and the 7-inch parts, leaving out the \( n \) five-inch parts.

stem: Which equation has no solution?
whyCorrect: An equation has no solution when the variable cancels and leaves a false statement. Subtracting x from both sides of x = x + 1 gives 0 = 1, which is never true, so no value of x works.

whyWrong.B: Subtracting x leaves 0 = x + 2, so x = −2 — exactly one solution.
whyWrong.C: Both sides are already identical, so every value of x works; that is infinitely many solutions, not none.
whyWrong.D: Subtracting x leaves 1 = x + 2, so x = −1 — one solution.

stem: \[ |15 - x| - 9 = 0 \]What are all positive solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Isolate the absolute value first: \( |15 - x| = 9 \). That splits into two equations, 15 − x = 9 and 15 − x = −9, giving x = 6 and x = 24. Both are positive, so both belong in the answer.

whyWrong.A: Both values are negative; substituting x = −6 gives \( |21| - 9 = 12 \), not 0.
whyWrong.B: −6 does not satisfy the equation, and the question asks only for positive solutions.
whyWrong.C: −24 does not satisfy the equation: \( |15 - (-24)| - 9 = 30 \).

stem: \[ ax - y = bxy \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( a \), \( b \), \( x \), and \( y \). Which equation correctly expresses \( a \) in terms of \( b \), \( x \), and \( y \)?
whyCorrect: Move the \( y \) to the right side first: \( ax = bxy + y \). Then divide both sides by \( x \), which is the only thing multiplying \( a \): \( a = \frac{bxy + y}{x} \). The \( -y \) becomes \( +y \) when it crosses over.

whyWrong.B: The sign on \( y \) is wrong — adding \( y \) to both sides makes it \( +y \) on the right, not \( -y \).
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal: it divides \( x \) by the other side instead of dividing the other side by \( x \).
whyWrong.D: Reciprocal and wrong sign, so both errors are present.

stem: The cost to rent a bus from Company X is $950 for the first 3 hours and an additional $50 per hour for each hour after the first 3 hours. If the total cost to rent the bus from Company X for \( t \) hours is $1,250, which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: The $950 is a flat charge that covers the first 3 hours, so it is added once, not multiplied. Only the hours beyond the third are billed at $50, and there are \( t - 3 \) of them. That gives 950 + 50(t − 3) = 1,250.

whyWrong.B: \( 3t \) is not the number of extra hours; it triples the total time instead of removing the first 3 hours.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies the flat $950 by the extra hours, charging it repeatedly, and then bills all \( t \) hours at $50 as well.
whyWrong.D: Both terms are wrong: the flat fee is multiplied by \( 3t \), and every hour is charged the hourly rate on top.

stem: \[ 6(x - 9) = 11(x - 9) \]What value of \( x \) is the solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Both sides are a multiple of the same quantity \( x - 9 \). Subtracting gives \( 5(x - 9) = 0 \), and since 5 is not zero, \( x - 9 = 0 \), so x = 9. Expanding works too but takes longer: 6x − 54 = 11x − 99 gives 45 = 5x.

stem: How many solutions does the equation 10x = 10 have?
whyCorrect: Dividing both sides by 10 gives x = 1, a single value. A linear equation with a nonzero coefficient on x always has exactly one solution.

whyWrong.A: There would be no solution only if the x terms cancelled and left a false statement, like 0 = 1.
whyWrong.C: Two solutions require a squared term or an absolute value; this equation is linear.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many solutions require both sides to be identical expressions, like 10x = 10x.

stem: \[ |6x - 3| = |5x| \]What is the smallest solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: When two absolute values are equal, the insides are either equal or opposite, so solve both. \( 6x - 3 = 5x \) gives x = 3, and \( 6x - 3 = -5x \) gives \( 11x = 3 \), so \( x = \frac{3}{11} \). Both check out in the original equation, and \( \frac{3}{11} \) is the smaller.

stem: \[ 9x + x = 2x + x + 5 \]Which of the following equations has the same solution as the given equation?
whyCorrect: Combine like terms on each side first: the left is 10x and the right is 3x + 5. Subtracting 3x from both sides gives 7x = 5.

whyWrong.B: The sign is wrong; moving 3x to the left leaves +5 on the right, since the 5 never moves.
whyWrong.C: 11x comes from adding the x terms across the equals sign instead of subtracting one side from the other.
whyWrong.D: Both errors at once — the x terms added rather than subtracted, and the constant's sign flipped.

note: The book prints "lies the same solution"; read as "has the same solution".

stem: \[ 12x = 65 - x \]What value of \( x \) is the solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Get every x term on one side by adding x to both sides: 13x = 65. Dividing by 13 gives x = 5.

stem: If 2x + 3 = 9, what is the value of 4x − 4?
whyCorrect: Solve for x first: 2x = 6, so x = 3. Then 4(3) − 4 = 8. A quicker route is to notice 4x is double 2x, so 4x = 12 and 4x − 4 = 8.

stem: If 2x + 3 = 9, what is the value of 4x − 4?
whyCorrect: From 2x + 3 = 9 you get 2x = 6, so x = 3, and 4(3) − 4 = 8. You can skip solving for x by doubling 2x = 6 to get 4x = 12.

stem: A veterinarian recommends that each day a certain cat should eat 24 calories per pound of the cat’s weight, plus an additional 14 calories. Which equation represents this situation, where \( c \) is the total number of calories the veterinarian recommends the cat should eat each day if the cat’s weight is \( x \) pounds?
whyCorrect: "Per pound" marks the number that multiplies the weight, so 24 is the coefficient of x. "An additional 14 calories" is a fixed amount added once, whatever the cat weighs, so it is the constant: c = 24x + 14.

whyWrong.A: This drops the extra 14 calories entirely.
whyWrong.B: Adding 24 and 14 into one rate makes the extra 14 calories scale with the cat's weight, which the stem does not say.
whyWrong.C: The roles are swapped: 14 is the flat addition and 24 is the per-pound rate, not the other way round.

stem: How many solutions does the equation 9x + 6 = 5x + 4x + 12 have?
whyCorrect: Combine the x terms on the right: 5x + 4x = 9x, so the equation reads 9x + 6 = 9x + 12. Subtracting 9x leaves 6 = 12, which is false, so no value of x satisfies it.

whyWrong.A: One solution would require different coefficients of x on the two sides; here they are both 9.
whyWrong.B: Two solutions need a quadratic or an absolute value; this equation is linear.
whyWrong.C: Infinitely many would need the constants to match as well, which would mean 6 = 6, not 6 = 12.

stem: Raheem bought 3 shirts that were each the same price. He used a coupon for $30 off the entire purchase. The cost for the entire purchase after using the coupon was $15. What was the original price, in dollars, for 1 shirt?
whyCorrect: Let p be one shirt's price. Three shirts cost 3p, and the coupon takes $30 off the whole purchase once, so 3p − 30 = 15. That gives 3p = 45 and p = 15. The coupon is not subtracted from each shirt.

stem: \[ 13x = 42 - x \]What value of \( x \) is the solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Add x to both sides to collect the x terms: 14x = 42, so x = 3.

stem: \[ |x - 9| + 81 = 99 \]What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Isolate the absolute value: \( |x - 9| = 18 \), so \( x - 9 = 18 \) or \( x - 9 = -18 \), giving x = 27 and x = −9. Their sum is 18. There is a shortcut worth remembering: the two solutions always sit the same distance either side of 9, so their sum is 2(9) = 18 no matter what the right-hand side is.

stem: The cost to rent a bus from Company X is $950 for the first 2 hours and an additional $50 per hour for each hour after the first 2 hours. If the total cost to rent the bus from Company X for \( t \) hours, where \( t > 2 \), is $1,250, which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: The $950 is charged once and already pays for the first 2 hours, so it is a constant, not a rate. The hours billed at $50 are the ones past the second, and there are \( t - 2 \) of them, giving 950 + 50(t − 2) = 1,250.

whyWrong.A: This multiplies the one-time $950 by the number of extra hours and then charges $50 for every hour as well.
whyWrong.B: Both terms are wrong: the flat fee is scaled by \( 2t \), and all \( t \) hours are charged the hourly rate.
whyWrong.D: \( 2t \) doubles the total time instead of removing the first 2 hours, so the extra hours are miscounted.

stem: Which equation has no solution?

whyWrong.C: The coefficients differ (\( -19x \) versus \( 19x \)), so the x terms do not cancel; solving gives x = 0.
whyWrong.D: The coefficients differ again, so there is exactly one solution, \( x = -\frac{1}{133} \).

stem: Raheem bought 9 shirts that were each the same price. He used a coupon for $54 off the entire purchase. The cost for the entire purchase after using the coupon was $108. What was the original price, in dollars, for 1 shirt?
whyCorrect: Let p be the price of one shirt. Nine shirts cost 9p, and the $54 coupon comes off the whole purchase once: 9p − 54 = 108. So 9p = 162 and p = 18. Do not subtract $54 from each shirt.

stem: How many solutions does the equation 6x + 4 = 6x + 8 have?
whyCorrect: Both sides have the same x term, so subtracting 6x leaves 4 = 8. That is false for every x, so the equation has no solution.

whyWrong.A: Infinitely many would require the constants to match too, as in 6x + 4 = 6x + 4.
whyWrong.B: Two solutions need a squared term or an absolute value; this is a linear equation.
whyWrong.C: Exactly one solution requires different x coefficients so that the x terms do not cancel.

stem: \[ 7x - 6x + 130 = 260 \]What value of \( x \) is the solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Combine the two x terms on the left before doing anything else: 7x − 6x is just x. The equation becomes x + 130 = 260, so x = 130.

stem: A teacher is creating an assignment worth 28 points. The assignment will consist of questions worth 1 point and questions worth 2 points. Which equation represents this situation, where \( x \) represents the number of 1-point questions and \( y \) represents the number of 2-point questions?
whyCorrect: Each variable counts questions, so multiply each count by what that question is worth: \( x \) questions at 1 point contribute \( x \) points, and \( y \) questions at 2 points contribute \( 2y \). The total must be 28, giving x + 2y = 28.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying the two counts together has no meaning here, and 3 is not a point value in the problem.
whyWrong.B: This charges every question 3 points, mixing the two point values into one.
whyWrong.C: The point values are attached to the wrong variables — this makes the 1-point questions worth 2 and the 2-point questions worth 1.

stem: How many solutions does the equation 5x + 3 = 5x + 7 have?
whyCorrect: The x terms are identical on both sides, so subtracting 5x removes them and leaves 3 = 7. That statement is false regardless of x, so no solution exists.

whyWrong.B: One solution requires the coefficients of x to differ so the x terms survive the subtraction.
whyWrong.C: Two solutions come from quadratics or absolute values, not from a linear equation.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many would require the constants to be equal as well, giving 3 = 3.

stem: \[ 13x + 50 = 180 \]Which equation has the same solution as the given equation?
whyCorrect: Subtract 50 from both sides — the same operation applied to each side preserves the solution. That gives 13x = 130.

whyWrong.A: This keeps the 50 and discards the 180, which changes the equation entirely.
whyWrong.B: 80 would come from 130 − 50, subtracting 50 twice.
whyWrong.D: This simply drops the +50 without subtracting it from the right side.

stem: Which equation has no solution?
whyCorrect: Expand each side and compare. In choice B the left is \( 3x - 3 \) and the right is \( -3(-x - 1) = 3x + 3 \). The x terms match but the constants do not, so subtracting \( 3x \) leaves \( -3 = 3 \), which is impossible.

whyWrong.A: \( -3(-x + 1) = 3x - 3 \), which is identical to the left side, so every x works.
whyWrong.C: \( 3x - 3 = 4x - 4 \) gives x = 1 — one solution, since the coefficients of x differ.
whyWrong.D: \( 3x - 3 = -4x + 4 \) gives \( 7x = 7 \), so x = 1 — again one solution.

stem: Sophia bought confetti and balloons for $56. Each package of confetti costs $3, and each balloon costs $1. If Sophia bought 10 packages of confetti, how many balloons did she buy?
whyCorrect: The confetti accounts for 10($3) = $30 of the $56, leaving $26 for balloons. Since each balloon costs $1, she bought 26 balloons.

stem: In 2010, a skating team had a total of 35 skaters, each classified as either advanced or intermediate. From 2010 to 2020, the number of advanced skaters on the team increased by approximately 53%, and the number of intermediate skaters on the team increased by approximately 44%. The total number of skaters on the team increased by approximately 49%. Which equation best represents this situation, where \( a \) represents the number of advanced skaters on the team in 2010 and \( b \) represents the number of intermediate skaters on the team in 2010?
whyCorrect: An increase of 53% means the 2020 count is 1.53 times the 2010 count, so the advanced group becomes 1.53a and the intermediate group 1.44b. Their sum is the 2020 total, which is 1.49 times the 2010 total of 35, i.e. 35(1.49). Matching each percentage to the group it describes is the whole question.

whyWrong.A: The 49% total growth is attached to the intermediate group, and the 44% is applied to the team total — the two rates are swapped.
whyWrong.B: 0.53b represents a 47% decrease, not a 53% increase, and the 49% is again misapplied to the advanced group.
whyWrong.D: The 53% and 44% rates are attached to the wrong groups: advanced grew by 53%, intermediate by 44%.

stem: The equation d = 33w + 100 gives the total amount of money \( d \), in dollars, that James plans to save \( w \) weeks after he starts to save. What is the total amount of money, in dollars, he plans to save in 10 weeks?
whyCorrect: Substitute w = 10 into the equation: d = 33(10) + 100 = 330 + 100 = 430. The 100 is money already there at week 0 and is added once, not per week.

whyWrong.A: 380 comes from using 33(10) + 50 or otherwise mishandling the constant.
whyWrong.C: 480 adds an extra 50; 33(10) is 330, not 380.
whyWrong.D: 530 comes from 43(10) + 100, adding the 100 into the weekly rate.

stem: Which of the following equations has exactly one solution?
whyCorrect: Exactly one solution requires the coefficients of x on the two sides to be different, so the x terms cannot cancel. Only choice B has \( +x \) on the left and \( -x \) on the right; solving gives \( 2x = -\frac{2}{44} \), so \( x = -\frac{1}{44} \).

whyWrong.A: Both sides have coefficient 1 on x, so subtracting x leaves \( \frac{1}{44} = 0 \) — no solution.
whyWrong.C: The two sides are identical, so every value of x works: infinitely many solutions.
whyWrong.D: Both sides have coefficient −1 on x, leaving \( \frac{1}{44} = 0 \) — again no solution.

stem: \[ 0.10x + 0.20y = 0.19(x + y) \]The equation gives a volume \( x \), in gallons, of a 10% saltwater solution that could be mixed with a volume \( y \), in gallons, of a 20% saltwater solution to produce a 19% saltwater solution. According to this equation, what volume, in gallons, of the 20% saltwater solution could be mixed with 50.0 gallons of 10% saltwater solution to produce a 19% saltwater solution? (Assume that the volume of the mixture is the sum of the volumes of the two solutions before they were mixed.)
whyCorrect: Substitute x = 50 and solve for y: 0.10(50) + 0.20y = 0.19(50 + y) becomes 5 + 0.20y = 9.5 + 0.19y. Subtracting 0.19y and 5 gives 0.01y = 4.5, so y = 450. The small coefficient 0.01 is why the answer is so large — 19% is very close to 20%, so the mixture must be mostly the 20% solution.

stem: \[ 4(x - 3) = 13 + 2(x - 3) \]If \( x \) is the solution to the given equation, what is the value of \( x - 3 \)?
whyCorrect: The quantity \( x - 3 \) appears on both sides, so treat it as one unknown \( u \): \( 4u = 13 + 2u \), giving \( 2u = 13 \) and \( u = 6.5 \). Since \( u \) is \( x - 3 \), that is already the answer — there is no need to find x.
note: Grid-in: 6.5 or 13/2.

stem: How many solutions does the equation 5x + 3 = 5x have?
whyCorrect: Subtracting 5x from both sides removes the variable and leaves 3 = 0, which is false. No value of x can make it true, so there is no solution.

whyWrong.B: One solution needs the x coefficients to differ; here both are 5.
whyWrong.C: Two solutions require a quadratic or absolute-value equation.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many would need the constants to agree too, as in 5x + 3 = 5x + 3.

stem: Casey is raising \( h \) horses and \( g \) goats. Each horse requires 2 acres of land, and each goat requires 1 acre of land. The \( h \) horses and \( g \) goats require 21 acres of land. Which equation represents this situation?
whyCorrect: Multiply each animal count by the acres that animal needs: horses take 2 acres each, so \( 2h \), and goats take 1 acre each, so \( g \). Their sum is the land used: g + 2h = 21.

whyWrong.A: The 2 is attached to the goats, which need only 1 acre each.
whyWrong.C: Dividing \( h \) by 2 says two horses share one acre, the opposite of needing 2 acres each.
whyWrong.D: Dividing \( g \) by 2 halves the goats' land instead of doubling the horses'.

stem: How many solutions does the equation \( 17(x - 16) = -16(x + 17) \) have?
whyCorrect: Expand both sides: the left is \( 17x - 272 \) and the right is \( -16x - 272 \), since \( 17 \times 16 = 16 \times 17 \). The constants happen to match, so they cancel and leave \( 33x = 0 \), i.e. x = 0 — one solution.

whyWrong.B: Two solutions require a quadratic or an absolute value; both sides here are linear.
whyWrong.C: Infinitely many would need the x coefficients to match as well, but 17 and −16 are different.
whyWrong.D: No solution would require the x terms to cancel and leave a false statement; here the x terms do not cancel.

note: The book prints "Infinetely" in choice C.

stem: How many solutions does the equation 7x − 19 = 19 − 7x have?
whyCorrect: The coefficients of x are 7 and −7, which are different, so the x terms do not cancel. Adding 7x and 19 to both sides gives 14x = 38, so \( x = \frac{19}{7} \) — exactly one solution. Any linear equation whose two sides have different x coefficients has exactly one solution, whatever the constants are.

whyWrong.A: No solution requires the x terms to cancel first, which needs identical coefficients.
whyWrong.C: Two solutions come from quadratics or absolute values, not from a linear equation.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many would need both sides to be the same expression; \( 7x - 19 \) and \( 19 - 7x \) are not.

stem: \[ 6(x - 4) = (x - 4) + 6 \]If \( x \) is the solution to the given equation, what is the value of \( x - 4 \)?
whyCorrect: Both sides are built from the same block \( x - 4 \), so call it \( u \): \( 6u = u + 6 \). Subtracting \( u \) gives \( 5u = 6 \), so \( u = \frac{6}{5} = 1.2 \), and \( u \) is what the question asks for.
note: Grid-in: 6/5 or 1.2.

stem: Raheem bought 9 shirts that were each the same price. He used a coupon for $54 off the entire purchase. The cost for the entire purchase after using the coupon was $108. What was the original price, in dollars, for 1 shirt?
whyCorrect: Nine shirts at price p cost 9p, and the coupon removes $54 from the whole purchase once: 9p − 54 = 108. So 9p = 162 and p = 18.

stem: If \( 9 - 4(4 - 9x) = 2 - 5(4 - 9x) \), what is the value of \( 4 - 9x \)?
whyCorrect: Do not expand the parentheses. Let \( u = 4 - 9x \), the block that appears twice: \( 9 - 4u = 2 - 5u \). Adding \( 5u \) and subtracting 9 gives \( u = -7 \), which is exactly the value asked for.

stem: \[ a(7x - 14) + 5a = 7(ax - 2a) - 35 \]In the given equation, \( a \) is a constant. The equation has infinitely many solutions. What are all possible values of \( a \)?
whyCorrect: Expand both sides. The left is \( 7ax - 14a + 5a = 7ax - 9a \); the right is \( 7ax - 14a - 35 \). The \( 7ax \) terms are identical whatever \( a \) is, so infinitely many solutions requires the constants to match too: \( -9a = -14a - 35 \), giving \( 5a = -35 \) and \( a = -7 \).

whyWrong.A: With a = 0 the equation becomes 0 = −35, which is false — no solutions at all, not infinitely many.
whyWrong.C: Only one value of \( a \) makes the constant terms agree; for every other value the equation reduces to a false statement.
whyWrong.D: There is a value that works, \( a = -7 \); substituting it makes both sides read \( 7ax - 63 \).

note: The book prints its last two choices both as "C)"; transcribed as C and D in printed order.

stem: \[ d = 15t \]The given equation relates the distance \( d \), in inches, of an object from its starting position to the time \( t \), in seconds, since the object started moving. What is the rate of change of the object’s distance from its starting position over time?
whyCorrect: In an equation of the form \( d = mt \), the rate of change is the coefficient \( m \) — the amount \( d \) changes each time \( t \) increases by 1. Here that coefficient is 15, so the object moves 15 inches per second.

whyWrong.A: \( 15t \) is the distance itself, not the rate; a rate must not depend on how long the object has been moving here.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{1}{15} \) inverts the relationship — it is seconds per inch, not inches per second.
whyWrong.D: This inverts the rate and keeps \( t \) in it, so it is neither a rate nor a constant.

stem: A rectangular region of land is divided into 40 square lots of equal area \( R \), in square units. The length of the region is 1.6 times the width of the region. If the width of the region is \( x\sqrt{R} \) units, what is the value of \( x \)?
whyCorrect: Each lot is a square of area \( R \), so each side is \( \sqrt{R} \), and the region is a grid of these squares. If the grid is \( w \) squares wide and \( \ell \) squares long, then \( w\ell = 40 \) and \( \ell = 1.6w \). Substituting gives \( 1.6w^{2} = 40 \), so \( w^{2} = 25 \) and \( w = 5 \). The width is therefore \( 5\sqrt{R} \), so x = 5.

stem:
A company that manufactures staplers calculates its monthly profit, in dollars, by subtracting its fixed monthly costs, in dollars, from its monthly sales revenue, in dollars. The equation
\[ 11{,}000 = 2.00x - 6{,}500 \]represents this situation for a month where \( x \) staplers are manufactured and sold. Which statement is the best interpretation of \( 2.00x \) in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The monthly sales revenue, in dollars, from selling \( x \) staplers

choices.label: B
choices.content: The monthly sales revenue, in dollars, from each stapler sold

choices.label: C
choices.content: The monthly cost, in dollars, of manufacturing each stapler

choices.label: D
choices.content: The monthly cost, in dollars, of manufacturing \( x \) staplers

whyCorrect: The stem says profit = revenue − fixed costs. Matching that to \( 11{,}000 = 2.00x - 6{,}500 \), the 11,000 is profit and the 6,500 is the fixed cost being subtracted, so the term left over, \( 2.00x \), must be the revenue — total revenue from all \( x \) staplers, since it carries the variable.

whyWrong.B: That describes 2.00 on its own, the revenue per stapler. Multiplying by \( x \) makes it a total, not a per-unit amount.
whyWrong.C: The only cost in the equation is the fixed 6,500; \( 2.00x \) is on the revenue side of the subtraction.
whyWrong.D: Again a cost, but \( 2.00x \) is being added to reach the profit, not subtracted, so it cannot be a cost.

stem: If 7 + x = 3, what is the value of 56 + 8x?
whyCorrect: Notice that 56 + 8x is exactly 8(7 + x). Since 7 + x = 3, the value is 8(3) = 24. Solving for x = −4 and substituting gives the same 24, just with more work.

stem: In one week in 2017, a technician earned a total of $1,055 by working at her regular job and at a second job doing part-time work. The equation 20h + 17c = 1,055 represents this situation, where \( h \) is the number of hours worked at her regular job and \( c \) is the number of hours worked at her second job. Which of the following is the best interpretation of 20 in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The amount, in dollars, the technician earned for each hour at her regular job

choices.label: B
choices.content: The amount, in dollars, the technician earned for each hour at her second job

choices.label: C
choices.content: The number of weeks the technician worked at her regular job

choices.label: D
choices.content: The number of weeks the technician worked at her second job

whyCorrect: A coefficient tells you the amount per one unit of the variable it multiplies. Here 20 multiplies \( h \), the regular-job hours, and the total is in dollars, so 20 is dollars per regular-job hour.

whyWrong.B: The second job's rate is 17, the coefficient attached to \( c \).
whyWrong.C: The equation counts hours, not weeks — the stem describes a single week.
whyWrong.D: Same problem, and 20 is not even attached to the second job's variable.

stem: If 7 + x = 4, what is the value of 42 + 6x?
whyCorrect: Factor 6 out of 42 + 6x to get 6(7 + x). Since 7 + x = 4, that is 6(4) = 24. Recognising the given expression inside the one you are asked about saves solving for x.

stem: \[ 2x - 3 = 2x \]How many solutions does the equation have?
whyCorrect: Both sides carry the same 2x, so subtracting it leaves −3 = 0, a false statement. No value of x can fix that, so there is no solution.

whyWrong.B: One solution requires different coefficients of x so that the variable survives.
whyWrong.C: Two solutions require a quadratic or an absolute value.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many would need the constants to match too, giving 2x − 3 = 2x − 3.

stem: A gym charges its members a one-time $34 enrollment fee and a membership fee of $16 per month. If there are no charges other than the enrollment fee and the membership fee, after how many months will a member have been charged a total of $178 at the gym?
whyCorrect: The $34 is charged once, so it is a constant: 34 + 16m = 178, where m is the number of months. Subtracting gives 16m = 144, so m = 9.

stem: What value of \( w \) is the solution to the equation 0.7w − 0.57 = 7(w − 0.001)?
whyCorrect: Distribute on the right first: 7(w − 0.001) = 7w − 0.007. Collecting w on one side gives 0.7w − 7w = −0.007 + 0.57, so −6.3w = 0.563 and \( w = -\frac{0.563}{6.3} = -\frac{563}{6300} \approx -0.0894 \).

stem: For a set of three consecutive integers, the result of subtracting the greatest integer from the sum of the other two integers is 48. What is the value of the greatest of the three integers?
whyCorrect: Call the integers n, n + 1 and n + 2, so the greatest is n + 2. The described quantity is \( [n + (n+1)] - (n+2) = n - 1 \), which equals 48, so n = 49. The question asks for the greatest, which is 49 + 2 = 51 — stopping at 49 is the trap.

stem: Which equation has no solution?
whyCorrect: Expand the right side of each choice and compare. In C, 9(7x + 16) = 63x + 144, so the equation says 63x + 360 = 63x + 144. The x terms cancel and leave 360 = 144, which is false, so nothing solves it.

whyWrong.A: 9(7x + 4) = 63x + 36, exactly the left side, so every x works — infinitely many solutions.
whyWrong.B: The coefficients 63 and 7 differ, so the x terms survive: 56x = 0 and x = 0.
whyWrong.D: The coefficients are 63 and −63, which differ, so there is one solution, \( x = -\frac{102}{126} \).

stem:
How many solutions does the equation
\[ 4(16x - 20) = -16(5 - 4x) \]have?
whyCorrect: Expand both sides: the left is \( 64x - 80 \), and the right is \( -80 + 64x \), which is the same expression written in the other order. Watch the sign on the right — \( -16 \) times \( -4x \) is \( +64x \). Since the two sides are identical, every real number is a solution.

whyWrong.A: One solution would require different coefficients of x; both sides give 64x.
whyWrong.B: Two solutions require a quadratic or absolute value; this equation is linear.
whyWrong.D: No solution would require the constants to differ after the x terms cancel, but both are −80.

stem:
\[ 5x + 4y = 44 \]
\[ 3x - 7y = 17 \]The solution to the given system of equations is \( (x, y) \). What is the value of \( 8x - 3y \)?
whyCorrect: Eliminate y: multiply the first equation by 7 and the second by 4 to get 35x + 28y = 308 and 12x − 28y = 68. Adding them gives 47x = 376, so x = 8, and substituting back into 5x + 4y = 44 gives y = 1. Then 8x − 3y = 64 − 3 = 61.

stem: \[ 2x - 2y = 2 \]One of the two linear equations in a system is given. The system has exactly one solution. Which equation could be the second equation in this system?
whyCorrect: Two lines meet at exactly one point when their slopes differ. Writing the given equation as y = x − 1 shows its slope is 1, so you need a second equation whose slope is not 1. Choice C rearranges to \( y = \frac{10}{8}x + \frac{5}{8} \), slope \( \frac{5}{4} \), so the lines cross once.

whyWrong.A: Dividing by 8 gives \( y = x + \frac{3}{8} \) — slope 1 with a different intercept, so the lines are parallel and there is no solution.
whyWrong.B: Dividing by 3 gives \( y = x - \frac{8}{3} \), again slope 1 and parallel.
whyWrong.D: This rearranges to y = x − 1, the same line as the given equation, so there are infinitely many solutions.

stem:
\[ 3x + 5y = 8 \]
\[ 9x + 15y = 24 \]For each real number \( r \), which of the following points lies on the graph of each equation in the \( xy \)-plane for the given system?
whyCorrect: The second equation is exactly 3 times the first, so the two graphs are the same line and any point on \( 3x + 5y = 8 \) works. Solving that for \( x \) gives \( x = \frac{8 - 5y}{3} = -\frac{5y}{3} + \frac{8}{3} \), so with \( y = r \) the point is \( \left(-\frac{5r}{3} + \frac{8}{3},\ r\right) \). Substituting confirms it: \( 3\left(-\frac{5r}{3} + \frac{8}{3}\right) + 5r = -5r + 8 + 5r = 8 \).

whyWrong.A: This solves for \( x \) but then writes the result as the \( y \)-coordinate; substituting gives \( \frac{-16r + 40}{3} \), not 8.
whyWrong.B: Solving \( 3x + 5y = 8 \) for \( y \) gives \( -\frac{3r}{5} + \frac{8}{5} \); the sign on the \( r \) term is wrong here, and substituting gives \( 6r + 8 \).
whyWrong.D: Substituting gives \( -\frac{2r}{3} + 144 \), which equals 8 only for one particular \( r \), not for every real number.
